## STEP 1 — PRE-COMMITMENT

**Causal Identification Strategy:**
The causal identification strategy relies on a difference-in-differences (DiD) framework, exploiting cross-state variation in the pre-Medicare uninsurance rate among the elderly. States with a higher proportion of uninsured elderly before Medicare's introduction (the "treatment intensity") are expected to experience a larger increase in health insurance coverage and, consequently, a larger "treatment" effect from Medicare. We will interact this state-level, time-invariant pre-Medicare uninsurance rate with a post-Medicare time dummy to estimate the aggregate effect of Medicare on total hospital spending per capita. State and year fixed effects will control for time-invariant state characteristics and common time trends, respectively.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Difference-in-differences exploiting cross-state variation in pre-Medicare elderly uninsurance rates — states with higher pre-Medicare uninsurance experienced a larger coverage shock when Medicare was introduced (continuous treatment intensity); comparing pre-Medicare (1948-1965) to post-Medicare (1966-1975) hospital spending trends across high vs. low pre-Medicare-uninsurance states

key_variables.treatment: pre-Medicare elderly uninsurance rate (continuous, state-level, measured in 1963); interacted with post-1966 indicator
key_variables.control: states with low pre-Medicare uninsurance (smaller coverage shock at Medicare's introduction)
key_variables.outcome: log total hospital spending per capita (all ages, not just elderly — to capture aggregate and spillover effects); also hospital beds, admissions, payroll per patient day

_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Medicare's introduction caused a large, statistically significant increase in total hospital spending that substantially exceeded the direct cost of insuring the elderly. A 10 percentage point higher pre-Medicare uninsurance rate is associated with approximately 4-5% higher total hospital spending growth post-Medicare. Critically, the increase in total spending (including non-elderly) is approximately 6x larger than the increase in elderly spending alone, indicating massive supply-side spillovers: hospitals expanded capacity, hired more staff, and adopted more technology in response to Medicare demand, raising costs for all patients.
_ground_truth.main_effect: 10pp higher pre-Medicare uninsurance rate → approximately 4-5% higher total hospital spending growth; supply-side spillovers account for ~85% of the total spending increase (aggregate effect ≈ 6× direct elderly spending increase)
key_robustness: Event-study specification showing no pre-trend in spending differences before 1966
Separating elderly vs. non-elderly spending (to isolate spillovers)
Alternative treatment variables (pre-Medicare physician supply, hospital bed supply)

identification_strategy_detail.method: DID with continuous treatment intensity: pre-Medicare elderly uninsurance rate × post-1966 indicator; state and year fixed effects
identification_strategy_detail.treatment: Cross-state variation in Medicare coverage shock (larger for states with higher pre-1965 elderly uninsurance rates)
identification_strategy_detail.estimation_window: Full panel 1948-1975; pre-trends tested on 1948-1965 data
identification_strategy_detail.key_assumption: Parallel trends: absent Medicare, hospital spending growth in high-uninsurance states would have followed the same trajectory as low-uninsurance states. Supported by event-study evidence showing no differential pre-trends in the 18 years before Medicare (1948-1965). Pre-Medicare uninsurance rates are not correlated with state-level spending trends.

key_magnitudes.total_spending_effect: +4-5% increase in total hospital spending per 10pp increase in pre-Medicare uninsurance rate
key_magnitudes.supply_side_multiplier: Aggregate spending increase is approximately 6x larger than the direct elderly spending increase
key_magnitudes.spillover_share: Supply-side spillovers (to non-elderly) account for approximately 85% of the total spending increase
key_magnitudes.hospital_capacity: States with bigger Medicare shocks saw larger increases in hospital beds and medical staff per capita

_ground_truth.robustness_notes_detail: Event-study analysis confirms parallel pre-trends over the 18-year pre-Medicare period (1948-1965). The spending increase begins precisely in 1966 (the year Medicare started) and grows over the subsequent decade, consistent with gradual hospital capacity expansion. Results survive controlling for Medicaid (introduced concurrently but with different cross-state variation) and for pre-existing differences in hospital supply. The 6× multiplier from supply-side spillovers implies that the true fiscal cost of Medicare was far larger than the actuarial cost of insuring the elderly alone.
